cases.abstract: Imitation policies trained on limited wrist-camera demonstrations can drift into states for which the training data provide no corrective action. DMD supplies corrective supervision by pairing synthesized nearby views with actions directed toward later poses on an expert trajectory. A pretrained, pose-conditioned diffusion model is adapted using task demonstrations, task-agnostic play, or both; reconstructed camera poses supply the geometry for labeling the generated views. Targeting a later frame avoids backward commands when a generated viewpoint has already passed the immediate successor. Real-robot evaluations span pushing, stacking, pouring, and shirt hanging. With 24 pushing demonstrations, DMD completes 10/10 trials versus 3/10 for behavior cloning. Augmentation also improves a Diffusion Policy trained with 1,447 cup-arrangement demonstrations, raising success from 4/25 to 16/25 on five unseen cups in a new laboratory. Both cup-arrangement policies use matched starts and the same cropped, rectified images. These comparisons support corrective augmentation beyond small datasets and across regression and diffusion policies. Its recovery assumption remains consequential: returning the camera to an expert pose cannot reverse spilled contents.
cases.methods: DMD's augmentation must change the action label as well as the image: a perturbed camera view need not warrant the command recorded at the original pose. Structure from motion first estimates camera poses along each demonstration, providing relative transforms between image pairs for adapting a pretrained, pose-conditioned diffusion model. The model then synthesizes views for sampled nearby virtual poses, and each generated view receives the transform from its virtual pose to a later demonstration pose as its action target. This ties visual perturbation to a command intended to resume progress. Using the immediate successor can instead direct the robot backward if the perturbation has overshot that pose. The implementation targets the third subsequent frame because directional-error improvement plateaus around that offset, while larger offsets discard more terminal frames. Generated pairs join the original data for policy training, under the assumption that these deviations remain recoverable.
cases.results: On held-out pushing trajectories, adding DMD to color jitter and horizontal flips lowers median directional error from 0.355 to 0.328 radians. In randomized robot trials with 24 demonstrations, DMD succeeds in 10/10 executions, compared with 3/10 for behavior cloning. The deployment comparison reveals a performance difference that the modest offline error reduction alone does not convey, consistent with small mistakes accumulating along a trajectory. With eight demonstrations, DMD achieves 8/10 successes versus 2/10 for behavior cloning, but its view generator is trained on separate play data, so that count excludes other training input. A separate cup-arrangement evaluation extends the comparison beyond scarce task data. On five unseen cups in a new laboratory, DMD improves a retrained Diffusion Policy from 4/25 to 16/25 successes using 1,447 demonstrations, matched starts, and identically cropped, rectified inputs. These cup results extend the observed benefit to diffusion policies. Nine trials still fail in the shifted setting, so expanded training coverage does not eliminate difficulties under object and environment shift.
cases.notes: Retained corrective labels as the central contribution; Methods connects pose perturbation to the command needed to recover. Results contrasts single-frame prediction with complete execution without treating their different metrics as a quantitative scaling relationship. The eight-demonstration policies use a generator trained on play data. Cup-arrangement comparisons use policies retrained for cropped, rectified inputs, not the original fisheye-input UMI system. Pouring comparisons remain omitted because task-only and task-plus-play outcomes came from different randomized A/B tests with different BC outcomes. Trial success counts are descriptive, not population guarantees.

cases.abstract: Fine bimanual manipulation couples two problems: collecting demonstrations with precise coordination and learning policies that remain effective over long, high-frequency trajectories. ALOHA provides an open-source teleoperation system assembled within a $20,000 budget. Direct joint-space coupling between smaller leader arms and larger follower arms avoids inverse-kinematics failures near singularities, while modified grippers support delicate contacts. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) learns from these demonstrations by predicting sequences of joint targets to reduce the effective decision horizon. Combining overlapping predictions for the same execution time retains frequent visual feedback without abrupt chunk transitions; conditional variational training models variation in human demonstrations. Evaluation covers two simulated and six physical tasks, with 50 demonstrations per physical task except threading, which uses 100. Over 25 trials per physical task and one training seed, ACT achieves 88% success opening an upright slider bag and 96% inserting a battery, compared with no final successes for four tuned imitation baselines. Autonomous velcro threading reaches only 20%. In a separate randomized study with six participants, average zip-tie threading time falls from 33 seconds at 5 Hz teleoperation to 20 seconds at 50 Hz.
cases.methods: ACT predicts a sequence of future joint targets from the current follower joint positions and four camera views. Its demonstration labels are leader targets, not follower positions, preserving the command discrepancies through which the position controller generates contact forces. Grouping targets into chunks is intended to shorten the effective horizon and represent temporally dependent human behavior, such as pauses within a chunk. Executing each chunk without new observations, however, would delay feedback and introduce abrupt transitions. ACT therefore queries the policy at every step and exponentially weights predictions from overlapping chunks only when they refer to the same execution time. This combines multiple estimates of one command rather than smoothing neighboring actions that may have different purposes. Conditional variational training separately represents variation among demonstrated sequences through a latent variable, reconstruction loss, and Gaussian-prior regularization. At deployment, the variational encoder is discarded and the latent variable is fixed at zero, producing deterministic predictions from observations.
cases.results: Without temporal ensembling, increasing ACT's chunk length from one to 100 actions raises mean success from 1% to 44% across two simulated tasks with scripted and human training data. Success then declines slightly for longer chunks: horizon reduction does not justify eliminating reactive feedback. Demonstration variability matters independently. Removing conditional variational training lowers success from 35.3% to 2% on human data, averaged across the two simulated tasks, but changes little on deterministic scripted data. This contrast supports using the objective with human demonstrations, not a uniform benefit across data sources. Temporal ensembling is also selective: separately tuned comparisons improve ACT and BC-ConvMLP while worsening VINN. Physical threading exposes a different bottleneck. In 25 physical trials from one training seed, ACT lifts the velcro tie in 92% of trials but completes threading in only 20%, despite 100 demonstrations. Premature gripper closure and missed insertions are consistent with difficulty localizing the thin, dark tie in camera images.
cases.notes: Kept ALOHA and ACT as complementary contributions; the abstract gives a hardware rationale and a separate human teleoperation comparison. Results connects chunk length and training objective to their intended roles, and retains the adverse VINN temporal-ensemble outcome with its separately tuned comparison. Physical threading means Thread Velcro, not the zip-tie user-study task. The 92%-to-20% stage contrast uses 25 physical trials and one training seed; simulation ablation aggregates are not assigned those counts. Candy unwrapping's 3/5 retry outcome is not a single-attempt rate. Hardware torque and gripper constraints remain separate from the reported localization errors.
